cards.explanation: The answer is that they do not lose heart. Paul says, “Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart.” The mercy comes first, and the not losing heart follows right behind it. I've lost heart in a dusty drawer before, friends, so I know that's no small thing.

The answer is False. Paul says, “We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God.” No bending and no trimming to make it more popular. Nobody gets a version with extra sprinkles on top, friends.

The answer is open. Paul says they commend themselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God “…by open proclamation of the truth…” Nothing tucked in the back and nothing whispered. That's the opposite of the secret and shameful ways they renounced, friends.

The answer is the light of the gospel. Paul says, “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” Picture a bakery with the ovens glowing and somebody standing there saying, "Is it dark in here?" The light is on, friends. The blinding is what keeps them from seeing it.

The answer is Jesus Christ as Lord. Paul says, “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” He points the spotlight at Jesus and steps out of it. That's a good example for all of us, friends.

The answer is servants. Paul says they proclaim “…Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” They're there for the Corinthians, and Jesus is the reason. Try putting that on a name tag, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says God “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” The light isn't just shining, friends, it's giving them knowledge. And that knowledge is of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

The answer is to show the power is from God. Paul says, “Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” Nobody looks at a plain old jar and gives the jar the credit. The jar is ordinary, friends, and the power belongs to God.

The answer is that trouble hits them but cannot break them. Paul says, “…hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair…” Every hard thing gets a “but not” right behind it. The trouble is real, friends, and it doesn't finish them.

The answer is False. Paul does use the word forsaken, but he says “…persecuted, but not forsaken…” He doesn't hide the hard part, friends, because they are persecuted. The "but not" is what makes the statement false.

The answer is True. Paul says, “We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.” That's a heavy line, friends, and it's worth sitting with for a second. Look where it ends up, though: the life of Jesus revealed.
The answer is life. Paul says, “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.” He doesn't dress up the first half, friends. Then he lands right on life.

The answer is True. Paul says they're knowing “…that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence.” Notice the word knowing, friends. It's not hoping and crossing fingers.
The answer is the Corinthians. Paul says God will “…present us with you in His presence.” The “you” is the Corinthians, the people he's writing to. It's a together thing, friends, not a solo trip.

The answer is thanksgiving. Paul says the grace extending to more and more people “…may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.” Overflow is my kind of word, friends. I've never met a cookie box I didn't overfill.

The answer is True. Paul says, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.” Wasting away on the outside, renewed on the inside. That beats any warranty card I ever read, friends, and I read a lot of them in a junk drawer.

The answer is an eternal weight of glory. Paul says, “For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.” Light and momentary sits right next to eternal weight, friends. He puts them side by side on purpose.

The answer is because what is unseen is eternal. Paul says, “For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.” That's his reason for fixing his eyes on what is unseen, friends. It's like watching a cookie timer when the batch you're really waiting on is the one that lasts forever.
